Media News Daily: Top Stories for 08/06/2026

TOPICS:Media News

Posted By: Media Bias Fact Check

This page hosts daily news stories about the media, social media, and the journalism industry. Get the latest Hirings and Firings, Media Transactions, Controversies, Censorship Issues, and more.

Trump Seeks to Block BBC From Financial Records

President Trump’s attorney filed an emergency motion to prevent the BBC from obtaining financial records connected to the Donald J. Trump Revocable Trust. The broadcaster received court approval last month to review financial documents after Trump claimed he suffered losses from a BBC Panorama episode titled “Trump: A Second Chance?” The lawsuit centers on an edited clip of Trump’s Jan. 6 speech that the BBC has apologized for but says was not defamatory. Trump’s attorney argued the subpoena is overly broad and seeks confidential tax, ownership, and financial records for roughly 400 entities, while the BBC says the information is relevant to Trump’s claims of financial harm. (Read More) (The Hill Rating)

Senator Says 60 Minutes Epstein Banking Story Vanished

Sen. Ron Wyden said a 60 Minutes investigation into Jeffrey Epstein’s banking relationships never aired after correspondent Sharyn Alfonsi left CBS News. Wyden said he sat for an interview with Alfonsi in March as part of a report examining how major financial institutions handled Epstein’s accounts and suspicious transactions. CBS confirmed the interview occurred but said the story was not completed before the season ended in May. The revelation came as Wyden released a Senate report accusing major banks of overlooking suspicious Epstein-related financial activity and criticizing the Trump administration for denying access to Treasury records tied to the investigation. (Read More) (Mediaite Rating)

OpenAI Settles Worker Discrimination Claims

OpenAI and a subsidiary will pay $3.2 million to settle Justice Department claims that they favored foreign workers with temporary employment visas and discriminated against U.S. job applicants. The Justice Department alleged that OpenAI and Statsig discouraged U.S. workers from applying for certain roles by using recruitment practices such as requiring paper applications, advertising jobs late at night on radio, and not posting openings externally. OpenAI denied wrongdoing but agreed to pay $1.2 million in penalties and $2 million to compensate alleged victims, revise employment policies, conduct training, and undergo Justice Department monitoring. (Read More) (The Guardian Rating)
